article_title: Speaking to Write: Examining Language Learners' Acceptance of Automatic Speech Recognition as a Writing Tool
citation: Johnson, C., & Cardoso, W. (2021). Speaking to write: examining language learners’ acceptance of automatic speech recognition as a writing tool. In N. Zoghlami et al. (Eds), CALL and professionalisation: short papers from EUROCALL 2021 (pp. 167-171). Research-publishing.net. https://doi.org/10.14705/rpnet.2021.54.1327
title: Use ASR-based writing to lift the burden of error-free form so learners can attend to content and other aspects of writing
description: Because ESL students often focus on linguistic form at the expense of content, context, genre, and process, the article proposes ASR dictation as a way to redirect attention: "Using ASR, a technology that converts speech to text, may remove some of the burden of producing error-free form, allowing students to pay attention to other aspects of writing such as content." The tool is free, accessible, and meets Chapelle's CALL criteria, including attention to meaning and authentic use. The article frames this as pedagogically promising but not yet tested for effectiveness.
requirements: Training on the ASR tool before use
Learners' speech intelligible to the technology
constraints: Pedagogical effectiveness not yet assessed; the authors state studies are needed to determine its true pedagogical potential and best practices for classroom implementation
target_learners: adult ESL writers in academic writing courses
target_learning_goals: attention to content, context, genre, and writing process rather than form alone
examples: Participants wrote authentic academic texts with ASR and reported focusing on getting the meaning of their ideas into texts without focusing on form
key_sources: Johnson, C., & Cardoso, W. (2021). Speaking to write: examining language learners’ acceptance of automatic speech recognition as a writing tool. In N. Zoghlami et al. (Eds), CALL and professionalisation: short papers from EUROCALL 2021 (pp. 167-171). Research-publishing.net. https://doi.org/10.14705/rpnet.2021.54.1327

article_title: Menu of Measures: High-Quality Measures of Middle Years Math Student Outcomes
citation: Julie Bruch, Jasmine Forde, Ijun Lai, Veronica Sotelo Muñoz. (2022). Menu of Measures: High-Quality Measures of Middle Years Math Student Outcomes. Mathematica. https://www.mathematica.org/publications/menu-of-measures-high-quality-measures-of-middle-years-math-student-outcomes
title: Assess measure quality with explicit criteria plus context-fit questions before adopting a measure
description: When choosing a measure of student outcomes, apply a set of quality criteria and then ask context-specific questions to judge fit. The resource "includes a set of criteria that can be used to assess measure quality, as well as context-specific questions to help readers determine if a specific measure is a good fit for their unique circumstances." Quality and fit are treated as distinct checks.
requirements: A defined set of measure-quality criteria
Context-specific questions about the adopting setting
constraints: Fit judgments depend on the reader's unique circumstances, so criteria alone do not guarantee fit
target_learners: middle grades math students
target_learning_goals: valid and reliable measurement of math outcomes
examples: The menu pairs its curated measure list with quality criteria and context-specific fit questions for educators, district leaders, researchers, and funders

article_title: Districts and Data: Developing Capacity for Effective Data Use
citation: Cassie Pickens Jewell, Libby Makowsky, Kristin Hallgren. (2014). Districts and Data: Developing Capacity for Effective Data Use. Issue Brief. Princeton, NJ: Mathematica Policy Research. https://www.mathematica.org/publications/districts-and-data-developing-capacity-for-effective-data-use
title: Ask the right questions and use data aligned with district goals
description: The brief's second key recommendation is to "Ask the right questions and use the correct data to support district goals." It observes that many districts do not know what questions to ask or what data to use, so question formulation and data selection are treated as capacities districts must deliberately develop. The recommendation ties data analysis directly to district improvement goals.

citation: Peter Z. Schochet. (2011). Do Typical RCTs of Education Interventions Have Sufficient Statistical Power for Linking Impacts on Teacher Practice and Student Achievement Outcomes? Journal of Educational and Behavioral Statistics, vol. 36, no. 4. https://www.mathematica.org/publications
title: Researchers should assess statistical power for mediator-outcome linkage analyses before relying on them to interpret RCT results
description: Because the article develops power formulas specifically for exploratory analyses linking teacher practice outcomes to student achievement outcomes in clustered school-based RCTs, it implies that researchers should evaluate power for these analyses when designing studies. The simulated power analysis exists to inform such assessments, indicating that typical RCTs may face power limitations for linking impacts on teacher practice and student achievement.

constraints: Applies to clustered school-based RCT designs using OLS or IV estimators
target_learners: Education researchers and evaluators
target_learning_goals: Designing adequately powered analyses of teacher practice mediators
examples: The article conducts a simulated power analysis to illustrate power for these linkage analyses in typical RCTs

article_title: Six insights regarding test-taking disengagement
citation: Steven Wise. (2021). Six insights regarding test-taking disengagement. Educational Research and Evaluation, 26(5-6), 328-338. https://www.nwea.org/research/
title: Assessment programs should attend to test-taking disengagement when interpreting scores
description: This principle holds that operators of assessment programs, particularly international assessment programs, should consider disengaged test taking when making and defending inferences from scores. The article's stated purpose is to discuss "six important insights yielded by this research and their implications for assessment programs", grounding the recommendation in evidence that disengagement distorts individual and aggregated scores and therefore the validity of country-level attainment inferences.
requirements: Assessment programs need methods for measuring disengagement to act on it
target_learners: Students in international and large-scale assessment programs
target_learning_goals: Valid interpretation of assessment scores at individual and aggregate levels
examples: The article derives implications for assessment programs from six research insights on disengagement

article_title: Unlocking the Potential of Technology Innovations: A Vision for Supporting Multilingual Learners
citation: Danae Kamdar, Tiffany Leones, Amanda LaTasha Armstrong, Shelton Daal & Ximena Dominguez. (2025). Unlocking the Potential of Technology Innovations: A Vision for Supporting Multilingual Learners. Digital Promise. https://digitalpromise.org
title: Asset-based, culturally and linguistically responsive design pattern for MLL edtech
description: This pattern treats multilingual learners' languages, cultures, and communities as assets to design around rather than obstacles, moving beyond simple translation. The report recommends that "efforts that move beyond simple translation and consider issues of cultural and linguistic sensitivity are needed." Interview exemplars include a studio that prioritized creating a product in Spanish first for Puerto Rican and Mexican communities before translating to English, recognizing that language and culture are interconnected, and recruiting a native speaker of the community as narrator so the community's language is authentically reflected.
requirements: Design teams must meaningfully include voices of MLLs, families, communities, and educators early and often throughout product development
Cultural and linguistic specificity must be addressed, since Spanish-speaking populations vary widely in cultural traditions and vocabulary
constraints: Interviewees noted that diversity among Spanish-speaking populations makes standardized best practices difficult and that addressing power dynamics among diverse team members takes time
target_learners: Young multilingual learners ages 3-8 and their families and communities
target_learning_goals: Engagement, comprehension, and enjoyment of learning content
Identity affirmation and authentic cultural and linguistic representation
examples: One studio developed a product for Spanish-speaking communities by designing in Spanish first, then translating to English; another recognized the need for a community native speaker as narrator during design

article_title: Teacher’s Roles in Supporting Collaborative Learning
citation: Judi Fusco, Sarah DiMaria, Beverly Yeadon, Linette Victor, Sarah Hampton, Janet Kolodner, London Jenks, Susan Yoon. (2024). Teacher's Roles in Supporting Collaborative Learning. Digital Promise. https://digitalpromise.org
title: Use an asset-based approach to classroom culture to balance status relationships and help students feel valued
description: Drawing on Bielaczyc and colleagues (2013) and Webb (2009), the primer recommends fostering a safe, supportive classroom culture by helping each student recognize the strengths and assets they bring to collaboration. As the primer explains, "an asset-based approach that highlights how each student plays an important role during collaboration helps balance status relationships among students by raising awareness of the multiple skills needed to accomplish the group task." Teachers should frequently discuss the importance of multiple abilities, comment on contributions of students who may be perceived as less important, and emphasize that no one person is best at every ability. The goal is a place where students feel valued and comfortable taking risks and sharing ideas.
requirements: Teachers must discuss the importance of multiple abilities and stress that all students bring important skills
constraints: The primer ties this to establishing trust through strong teacher-student relationships, which research links to engagement, attendance, grades, and lower dropout rates
target_learners: K-12 students in collaborative groups, including students perceived as less important to their groups
target_learning_goals: Willingness to take risks, share ideas, and work together during collaborative learning
examples: The primer cites Webb (2009) on teachers discussing multiple abilities and commenting on contributions of students perceived as less important to the group

article_title: Introduction to Culturally Responsive Assessment: A Graduate Course Design Guide
citation: Culturally Responsive Assessment Collaborative. (2025, November). Introduction to Culturally Responsive Assessment: A Graduate Course Design Guide. Digital Promise. https://doi.org/10.51388/20.500.12265/276/
title: Design assessment as a coherent system aligned with learning goals and equity outcomes
description: When assessment is defined as a system rather than a single test, the guide's coherence principle requires that all components—from individual items to high-stakes policy measures—align with contemporary models of learning and the equity outcomes of the broader curriculum and program context. In CRA, this means externally developed instruments must be intentionally designed to support the culturally responsive teaching and learning occurring in the local environment. No single test can be the sole driver of equity and improvement; the system's role is to complement broader instructional, community, and aspirational goals.
requirements: All components of the assessment system must align with contemporary models of learning and the desired learning goals and equity outcomes of the overarching curriculum
constraints: Externally developed assessment instruments require intentional design to fit the local culturally responsive context
target_learners: assessment developers and graduate measurement students
target_learning_goals: design coherent assessment systems that support culturally responsive teaching and equity
examples: The guide cites Evans et al. (forthcoming), Glaser et al. (2001), and Marion et al. (2024) on coherence in assessment systems

a problem bank supporting mastery-oriented practice

article_title: Developing a Stealth Assessment System Using a Continuous Conjunctive Model
citation: Jiaqi Yu, Wenchao Ma, Jewoong Moon, Andre R. Denham. (2022). Developing a Stealth Assessment System Using a Continuous Conjunctive Model. Journal of Learning Analytics, 9(3), 11–31. https://doi.org/10.18608/jla.2022.7639
title: Implement evidence-based assessment models at the early stage of educational game development to enable task-specific stealth assessment
description: The article argues that stealth assessment should be built into a game from the start rather than retrofitting analytics onto pre-existing games. It notes it is "hard to track players' mastery of content knowledge due to the lack of task-specific data across the game levels" when using pre-existing games, and that researchers have promoted "implementing evidence-based assessment models at the early stage of game development". The Nomads was designed with task-specific tracking and a CCM so that randomly generated items could yield diagnostic skill profiles.
requirements: Game tasks mapped to skills via a Q-matrix determined by subject experts
An event-based logging system recording each completed item's skills, correctness, timing, and scaffold use
constraints: Building a DGBL application with a learning analytics system from scratch is costly and time-consuming, per the article
target_learners: K-12 students playing educational mathematics games
target_learning_goals: Unobtrusive measurement of skill mastery during gameplay
Diagnostic skill profiles that inform learning support
examples: The study's team designed and developed The Nomads from scratch with nine task types, embedded scaffolds, and log parameters aligned to five attributes before collecting data.

article_title: Integrating Social, Emotional, and Academic Development (SEAD)
citation: Integrating Social, Emotional and Academic Development: An Action Guide for School Leadership Teams. (2019). Aspen Institute. https://hthgse.edu/empathy-interviews-learn-about-the-problem-from-a-users-perspective/
title: Use existing staff and time more strategically before adding new SEAD programs or positions
description: The guide's asset-mapping principle holds that schools should inventory and realign all resources—staff, time, technology, space, community assets, and budget—around their vision before purchasing new programs. It argues that traditional add-on approaches are "insufficient because it rarely attends to the classroom teachers that comprise over 80% of a typical school's budget," and that "Identifying opportunities to use existing staff and time more strategically should come before making additional investments." Resource equity means allocating by need rather than giving every student the same thing.
requirements: A full asset map of resources inside and outside the school, including community assets such as after-school care, health centers, and nonprofits
constraints: New positions created through trade-offs may lack content-team colleagues and need district professional-learning support
target_learners: All students, with resource decisions based on need
target_learning_goals: Equitable access to social, emotional, and academic development supports
examples: Rogers' school eliminated teaching assistant positions and hall monitors to fund a floating science teacher and expanded planning time

article_title: Cost and Cost Effectiveness of ASSISTments Online Math Support: Analysis from a Randomized Controlled Study in Middle School
citation: Feng, M., Weiser, G., & Collins, K. (2024). Cost and cost effectiveness of ASSISTments online math support: Analysis from a randomized controlled study in middle school. WestEd. https://www.wested.org
title: ASSISTments online math homework platform
description: ASSISTments is a free, web-based platform used in the study as an online tool for math homework, with many teachers also using it for classwork. It "provided students with instant feedback on their math work, while teachers received real-time data and progress reports on student learning." The platform contains textbook-based problems from schools' existing curricula plus prebuilt content, and developers built teacher-created practice problems into it on request. No specialized hardware or software was required beyond existing devices.
requirements: Teachers are expected to assign ASSISTments assignments for 20-30 minutes at least twice a week and regularly review data reports of student work
constraints: The platform itself is free, but effective implementation in the study required professional development, a local coach, and modest technology support for account setup
target_learners: seventh-grade middle school math students
target_learning_goals: middle school mathematics achievement
examples: In the North Carolina RCT, intervention teachers implemented ASSISTments over two consecutive school years with 2-day summer professional development and coaching visits averaging three per teacher per year

article_title: Accelerate English Learner Success: Students Take Ownership over Their Learning with Formative Assessment
citation: Barbara Jones, Molly Faulkner-Bond, and Jennifer Blitz. (2024). Accelerate English Learner Success: Students Take Ownership Over Their Learning With Formative Assessment. Region 15 Comprehensive Center at WestEd. https://www.wested.org/
title: Quality instruction for English learners promotes asset-based teaching, learning, and assessment grounded in funds of knowledge and identity
description: The brief's second feature holds that students' knowledge, experience, and sensibilities are critical assets for gaining new knowledge and skills. Asset-based instruction prioritizes what students can do rather than what they can't yet do, rooted in students' funds of knowledge—abilities passed down through generations—and funds of identity. Teachers build instruction around student-specific funds (interests, talents, passions) and community funds (collective histories, activities, norms, values).
requirements: Teachers must develop an understanding of their students' families, communities, cultures, and interests in ways that establish and sustain relationships.
constraints: The brief notes this sociocultural focus is particularly important for learners from culturally and linguistically diverse backgrounds, who may otherwise experience a sociocultural disconnect from classroom activities and settings.
target_learners: English learners and their non-English learner peers
target_learning_goals: Meaningful, culturally responsive learning that leverages students' rich experiences as a catalyst for developing learning
examples: Teachers can gather evidence by asking students to journal and write stories about their families in their first language and in English, bring in collections of significant items, make videos, take photographs, and draw self-portraits.

article_title: Scaling Teachers' Professional Development for ASSISTments Companion Report: Implementation Analysis of the ASSISTments Intervention
citation: Feng, M., Li, L., Brezack, N., & Schneider, M. (2025). Scaling teachers' professional development for ASSISTments companion report: Implementation analysis of the ASSISTments intervention. WestEd. https://www.wested.org
title: ASSISTments platform with the four steps of formative assessment
description: ASSISTments is "a free, web-based formative assessment platform for teachers and students in grades 3 through 12" that delivers immediate feedback, hints, explanations, and step-by-step scaffolds while generating color-coded class- and student-level reports. Its use is standardized into four steps of formative assessment: Assign standards-aligned problem sets, Practice with immediate feedback, Assess reports to identify patterns and errors, and Review selected problems using anonymized projected data. The intervention paired the platform with a virtual professional learning community to train rural middle school teachers.
requirements: Teachers need initial training and ongoing support to use the platform effectively following the four steps
constraints: Home internet or device access limits out-of-school use, so the study found in-class use more equitable
target_learners: middle school students in grades 6–8, particularly in rural and underresourced schools
target_learning_goals: middle school mathematics achievement
formative assessment practices
examples: Teachers assigned regular assignments and Skill Builders, with 70% of assignments being regular assignments rather than Skill Builders

article_title: Scaling Teachers' Professional Development for ASSISTments Companion Report: Implementation Analysis of the ASSISTments Intervention
citation: Feng, M., Li, L., Brezack, N., & Schneider, M. (2025). Scaling teachers' professional development for ASSISTments companion report: Implementation analysis of the ASSISTments intervention. WestEd. https://www.wested.org
title: Virtual professional learning community (vPLC) for ASSISTments teacher training
description: The vPLC is a virtual professional learning model designed to connect rural and geographically isolated teachers with peers and learning opportunities. It consisted of eight 75-minute virtual facilitated sessions during the school year, supplemented by asynchronous activities, led with three core goals: supporting effective ASSISTments use following the four steps, engaging teachers in analysis-of-practice, and modeling NCTM norms of excellent math teaching. Teachers responded positively: most (87%) participated fully, and about half rated the vPLC as comparable to or better than other professional development they had experienced.
requirements: Trained facilitators, a facilitation guide, and session structures such as breakout-room discussions with peer teachers
constraints: Designed for teachers with limited access to in-person PLCs; rural vPLCs are more effective when flexible, interactive, relevant, and ongoing, per the article's cited research
target_learners: rural middle school math teachers and teachers lacking peer networks or in-person professional learning access
target_learning_goals: effective use of ASSISTments and the four steps of formative assessment
data-informed math instruction
professional community building
examples: Session themes included using ASSISTments data and common wrong answers to inform instruction and framing mistakes as part of learning

citation: Feng, M., Li, L., Brezack, N., Huang, C.-W., Luttgen, K., Grady, J., Yang, S., Lavine, A., Collins, K., & Schneider, M. (2025). Scaling teachers' professional development for ASSISTments: Evaluation final report. WestEd. https://WestEd.org
title: ASSISTments platform: student-facing independent practice with immediate feedback and mastery-based Skill Builders, plus teacher-facing real-time reports

Students complete regular assignments built from OER curriculum problems (Illustrative Math, EngageNY) and mastery-oriented Skill Builders, receiving "immediate feedback on the correctness of answers"; they "cannot proceed to the next problem until they have correctly solved the current one". Teachers view real-time grid-format reports showing per-question accuracy, common wrong answers, and individual student responses, which they use to target instruction and form groups.
requirements: Students need technology access allowing internet-based classwork and homework, an eligibility condition the study states for participating teachers' students.
constraints: Full credit is awarded only for independent solving; partial credit is given when students use hints or require multiple attempts.
target_learners: Middle school students in grades 6-8
target_learning_goals: Mathematics achievement, including conceptual understanding, procedural skill/fluency, and application
examples: In the study treatment condition, teachers were asked to assign prebuilt content at least three times per week for 17 weeks using a combination of regular assignments and Skill Builders.

article_title: Making Assessment Reports More Meaningful for Students & Families
citation: Levitan, S., & Munyan-Penney, N. (2024). Meaningful Assessment Reporting: Making Assessment Reports More Meaningful for Students & Families. EdTrust. https://edtrust.org/
title: Use asset-framing in assessment reports so results acknowledge system responsibility and student strengths rather than deficit labels
description: The brief holds that "asset-based language and beliefs are fundamental to strong assessment reporting." Asset-framed reports explicitly acknowledge system-level responsibility for providing supports, highlight students' strengths and capabilities, and avoid deficit language such as "student cannot" in favor of phrases like "has yet to demonstrate" or "may need support in." title: Signaling function of large-scale assessments as a driver of instructional experiences
description: The report describes signaling as the mechanism by which large-scale assessments shape instruction: rich performance tasks provide concrete examples and direct experiences of the kinds of learning opportunities students should have, signaling to educators and leaders the instruction needed to prepare students to complete such tasks. It argues assessment systems frequently make their biggest mark on instruction through this signaling function, influencing what gets taught and what success looks like. The cascade of signals grows as districts adopt predictive interim assessments and item banks mirroring state questions.

constraints: The report presents signaling as an authors' interpretation of how assessments influence instruction, not a tested causal result

target_learning_goals: deeper learning
disciplinary practices
higher-order thinking and problem-solving
examples: Performance tasks in large-scale programs signal features of effective learning environments and, when curriculum-embedded, provide actual classroom experiences

article_title: What Changes When the Interlocutor Is an AI? Interactional Fluency and Linguistic Uptake in L2 Spoken Dialogue
citation: Russell Scheinberg, Ameeta Agrawal, Tetyana Sydorenko, Kalab Kahsay, Nina Vyatkina, Griet Boone. (2026). What Changes When the Interlocutor Is an AI? Interactional Fluency and Linguistic Uptake in L2 Spoken Dialogue. https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.22225
title: Transcript-based pipeline for measuring interactional fluency and direction-sensitive uptake from diarized ASR output
description: A reusable analysis pipeline that operationalizes interactional fluency and direction-sensitive linguistic uptake for spoken AI practice "using metrics extractable from diarized ASR output without manual linguistic annotation." The fluency component extracts seven features from word-level timestamps (conversation length, turn count, mean turn duration, words per turn, response latency, floor ratio, within-turn pause ratio). The uptake component tracks lexical adoption via a global timeline with a first-use, first-source-wins rule, and syntactic uptake via four German morphosyntactic template types parsed with the Stanza UD pipeline, with correctness checked against a 91,270-noun gender lexicon. The authors provide it as "a reusable analysis pipeline for rapid, scalable evaluation of conversational AI in educational settings."
requirements: Diarized, timestamped ASR transcripts with verified speaker labels; a baseline monologue preceding each dialogue to establish learner-specific vocabulary baselines
constraints: Transcript-based analysis excludes prosody, pronunciation, stress, intonation, and segmental accuracy
NLP pipelines trained on Standard German may degrade on disfluent L2 speech; word-level ASR errors were not systematically corrected
target_learners: second- and third-year university L2 German learners
target_learning_goals: measuring interactional fluency and linguistic uptake in L2 spoken dialogue practice
examples: Applied to 78 AI dialogues and 39 human-human conversations from four sites, with three AI transcripts' speaker label swaps corrected via a disfluency-rate classifier

citation: Yi Zhang & Julia Rayz. (2026). From Execution to Education: A Bloom-Aligned Framework for Measuring Educational Control in LLMs. Preprint. https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.08009

description: The article argues that excelling at execution benchmarks shows a model can be a proficient problem solver without being an effective educator, and that optimizing solely for functionally correct solutions can cause an "illusion of learning". It recommends that "when deploying LLMs as educational tools, we should look beyond valid problem-solving and actively assess whether a model can recognize educational frameworks, adjust cognitive complexity, and intentionally mutate tasks for different learners." article_title: Cognitive offloading and the speedup illusion in human-AI interaction
citation: Sunny Yu, Myra Cheng, Ahmad Jabbar, Ilia Sucholutsky, Katherine M. Collins, Dan Jurafsky, Robert D. Hawkins. (2026). Cognitive offloading and the speedup illusion in human-AI interaction. arXiv. https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.23177
title: Asymmetric miscalibration account of cognitive offloading to AI (the speedup illusion framework)
description: The article proposes that offloading decisions require calibration — an accurate mental model of one's own and the tool's capabilities — and that for LLMs this calibration is asymmetric: people are "accurate in their prediction of the completion time" for independent work but systematically underestimate AI-assisted time. Grounded in the metacognitive access argument, it holds that people lack privileged access to an LLM's internal workings, and that effort-time conflation sustains the illusion. The framework positions calibration as both a subject and a mechanism for studying AI use.
requirements: Applies to simple cognitive tasks completable under 5 minutes with current LLM assistants; the article notes the complexity level at which AI genuinely saves time is an open question
constraints: Based on between-subjects aggregates with crowdsourced participants; the prediction and completion samples were not completely disjoint
target_learners: US adult Prolific participants completing simple cognitive tasks
target_learning_goals: Accurate calibration of when AI assistance saves time versus effort in cognitive offloading decisions
examples: The study operationalized calibration as the gap between predicted and actual completion times across 24 tasks in four categories of LLM use at two difficulty levels.

citation: Alonso-Carracedo, M., Fernandez-Boullon, R., Celard, P., Rodríguez-Martínez, F. J., & Otero-Cerdeira, L. (2026). CogTax: A Four-Level Cognitive Taxonomy for Command-Line Computing Education. arXiv. https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.00140
title: AST-based structural command representation using bashlex parse trees, tree metrics, and TF-IDF weighted n-grams
description: A structural representation pipeline that parses Linux/bash commands into abstract syntax trees using bashlex and extracts features from the trees. The article explains that "each command is additionally represented by the multiset of ordered pairs(parent_label, child_label)extracted from the AST," alongside ten numeric tree metrics (node count, depth, max width, leaf count, branching factor, pipelines, operators, redirects, commands, subshells) and TF-IDF weighted n-grams (n = 1 to 4) over the DFS preorder node-kind sequence. This abstracts away lexical content such as file names and arguments, retaining structural relationships that determine command behaviour.
requirements: Valid Linux/bash commands parseable by bashlex; standard scaling of numeric metrics
constraints: Purely syntactic analysis cannot distinguish commands with identical syntax but different operational semantics, such as structurally identical L1 and L2 commands
target_learners: computing education researchers and instructors classifying commands
target_learning_goals: automatic assignment of taxonomy levels from command syntax

citation: Jiatong Liu, Xue Yao, Zehua Zhang, and Yongqiang Tian. (2026). DebugTracker: Lightweight Process Evidence for Classroom Debugging. title: Assess the debugging process, not only the final patch, because identical final code can hide different debugging competence
description: Classroom assessment that considers only the submitted code and pass/fail test result creates a process-visibility gap: the intermediate steps of reproducing, narrowing, hypothesizing, and verifying leave no durable record. The article argues that "the final code can look identical even when the underlying debugging competence differs", so feedback that ignores the process misses what the exercise was meant to assess. Recording the reproduce-observe-hypothesize-edit-verify chain makes that process reviewable.
requirements: A lightweight, structured record of the debugging process that is cheap to produce, cheap to read, and bounded to the task at hand
constraints: Screen recording and live observation capture the process faithfully but do not scale to large cohorts, are intrusive, and collect far more data than a review task requires; commit history is too coarse and easily rewritten
target_learners: Novice programmers in classroom debugging exercises
target_learning_goals: Systematic debugging investigation rather than lucky guessing or repeated edit-and-test flailing
examples: The article contrasts two students who both submit a passing solution: one may have followed an evidence-based debugging process while the other edited and tested repeatedly until the suite turned green

title: Differentiated framework of assistive versus content-generative AI use
description: The article's organizing analytical distinction separates two modes of student engagement with generative AI. As the authors state, "AI mayfunctionasassistivesupportwhenstudentsuseitforideation, referencegathering,processmanagement,reﬁnement,ortechnique learning. It may function diﬀerently when it contributes directly to the content of the ﬁnal work." Assistive use scaffolds students' own creative decisions, while content-generative use enters the authorship of the work itself. The framework is operationalized through two questionnaire indicators, ai_help_pct and ai_content_pct, capturing augmentation-oriented versus substitution-oriented usage.

article_title: Student GenAI use under changing institutional policies: a mixed-methods case study in undergraduate physics
citation: Zachery Quince and Emily Faulconer. (2026). Student GenAI use under changing institutional policies: a mixed-methods case study in undergraduate physics. International Journal of STEM Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s40594-026-00651-w
title: Design assessments so that task demands, not policy labels, shape which GenAI functions students use
description: The article argues that a purpose-specific or open-use policy label defines what is permitted but cannot determine how students use GenAI; the assessment itself creates the demand. It concludes that "assessment design shapes which GenAI functions become meaningful": tasks rewarding polished communication elicit language and structure uses, while problem-solving tasks elicit checking, clarification, and verification uses. Assessment design that rewards understanding and requires student judgement aligns with the markers of evaluative judgement, keeping constructive alignment intact in the GenAI era.
requirements: Assessment tasks that require application of concepts to real-world scenarios and student judgement
constraints: The study is a single case with limited generalisability and does not establish a causal link between policy and outcomes; confounds include learning progression, tool familiarity, and task complexity
target_learners: undergraduate STEM students
target_learning_goals: maintaining constructive alignment and evaluative judgement when GenAI is available
examples: A1's presentation task made planning, language, and structure support relevant; A2's workbook and A3's quiz made checking, clarification, and verification relevant

title: Assessment twins: two deliberately linked assessment components addressing the same outcomes through different modes of evidence
description: The article names and substantively describes assessment twins as a redesign approach for the GenAI era. Twins are conceptualised as "two deliberately linked components that address the same learning outcomes through different modes of evidence, scheduled closely together to allow for cross-verification". The pairing lets instructors triangulate evidence across formats so that validity can be checked even when one format is vulnerable to generative AI misuse.

citation: Sunaina Sharma. (2026). Educational integrity in GenAI-augmented assessment: making judgement visible. International Journal for Educational Integrity 22:6. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40979-026-00216-y
title: Design assessment so that integrity is enacted through transparent, justified decision-making rather than inferred from technological absence
description: The paper's central design principle: assessment should be reconceptualized as the primary site where educational integrity is enacted, shifting attention "from whether GenAI was used to how academic choices were made and responsibility exercised". Assessment structures that foreground decision-making, transparency, and justification render integrity visible within hybrid human-GenAI work and scaffold accountability instead of relying on surveillance.

Educators need shared criteria and professional calibration to interpret articulated judgement consistently

citation: Vega-Baudrit JR and Rivera Álvarez A (2026) Generative artificial intelligence in university chemistry education: a critical review using Johnstone’s chemistry triplet and Biggs’ 3P model. Front. Educ. 11:1918707. https://doi.org/10.3389/feduc.2026.1918707
title: Make verification an assessed activity, not merely a recommendation
description: This principle holds that verification of GenAI outputs should be built into assessment so that chemical judgment, not fluent production, is the assessed construct. The review states that "Verification should be assessed, not merely recommended" and that student reasoning should remain visible through prompt logs, annotated outputs, drafts, calculations, oral defense, and revision histories. Evidence of thinking such as prompt logs, intermediate calculations, and revision histories must be preserved
constraints: A generic recommendation to verify AI output is insufficient without chemistry-specific checks

target_learning_goals: Chemical judgment and verification skills
Independent reasoning in AI-supported tasks
examples: The review describes verification-centered assessment in which students identify an AI error, defend a correction, compare alternative representations, reproduce reasoning without AI, or explain why a generated answer should be rejected

citation: Yusuf Pisan. (2026). Teaching Intro AI When the Tools Can Do the Homework: A Course Redesign and a Student Bill of Rights. https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.05175
title: Assessment without examinations: weight moved to in-class exercises, reflective writing, and a defended team project that resist unattributed automation
description: This pattern rebuilds grading around tasks a language model cannot quietly ghost-write, on the bet that "an assessment a model can silently complete is a weak assessment." The Spring 2026 grade comprised in-class exercises done in the room in a fixed hour (20 percent), weekly projects that may be reflection, programming, or a mix (40 percent), and a team project (40 percent), with no midterm or final. Reflective writing carries a first-person account of the student's own process, and in-class exercises were graded complete-or-incomplete on submission with AI scores advisory only.
requirements: In-class exercises require a fixed scheduled hour in the room and produce an artifact on the spot
Reflective writing must be required to be in the student's own voice
constraints: The author's own students, asked to design fair grading for such a course, mostly reinvented proctored or handwritten assessment, the strongest internal challenge to this structure
The author makes no causal or learning-outcome claims for the structure

target_learning_goals: artificial intelligence fundamentals
engineering judgment and supervision of AI tools
reflective practice

citation: Zhaozhe Wang, Chaoran Wang. (2025). A posthumanist approach to AI literacy. Computers and Composition 76 (2025) 102933. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.compcom.2025.102933
title: Assemblage and rhizomaticity as posthumanist concepts for AI-mediated literacy
description: The article deploys Deleuze and Guattari's assemblage and rhizomaticity, elaborated by Bennett, Leander and Burriss, and Sherman et al., to explain how posthumanist relationality plays out in AI-mediated literacy. An assemblage is "always temporarily formed as diverse human agents, nonhuman actants, discourses, and signs come into contact and relate to one another," and assemblages operate rhizomatically, shifting and reconfiguring in any direction. Literacy practices are conceived as forming assemblages in which AI may partake, co-producing meaning with human writers.

citation: Sireci, S. G., Tucker, E. M., & Gordon, E. W. (Eds.). (2025). Handbook for Assessment in the Service of Learning, Volume II: Reconceptualizing Assessment to Improve Learning. University of Massachusetts Amherst Libraries. https://openpublishing.library.umass.edu/
title: Gordon's transactional troika: assessment, teaching, and learning as inseparable, mutually reinforcing processes
description: Gordon proposes that assessment, teaching, and learning form a dynamic, dialectical system rather than separate stages of education. He writes that he describes them "as a kind of troika or three-legged stool: each element supports and strengthens the others, and none should function independently of the whole." In this transactional view, an assessment is a two-way exchange in which the student is an active agent who interprets tasks, uses feedback, and brings identity and feeling into the interaction. The handbook series is organized around this reconceptualization, treating assessment as embedded in pedagogy rather than as an external verdict passed on learning after the fact.
requirements: Assessment must be implemented in a supportive, trustful environment so it feels like an extension of teaching rather than a judgment from on high
constraints: The authors frame this as a vision requiring institutional change; conventional high-stakes testing regimes currently operate outside this paradigm
target_learners: All learners across preK-12, higher education, workplace, and informal settings
target_learning_goals: Intellective competence and human development
examples: Gordon cites Feuerstein's instrumental enrichment tasks, which functioned as assessments and interventions at once

description: The principle holds that assessments should be crafted as rich problems, projects, or simulations that both elicit evidence of learning and produce it. description: The article argues that assessing non-social cognitive traits in a non-social manner may provide a fair way to assess both autistic and neurotypical candidates' readiness for the same job. title: Associative-network interference account of arithmetic fact retrieval
description: The article works within the theoretical account that arithmetic facts are stored in an associative network in semantic memory, so that retrieving one fact activates competing facts that must be inhibited. It states that "arithmetic facts are particularly prone to interference" because of shared features, and that poor inhibition could yield specific errors such as answering 6 × 3 = 24. This framework motivated the study's hypothesis that cognitive inhibition would relate to fact retrieval, a hypothesis the data did not support in typically developing children.
requirements: The account presupposes that competing problem-answer associations are formed and stored in long-term memory during fact learning
constraints: The present study's data did not support the predicted inhibition–fact-retrieval association in typically developing third graders
target_learners: typically developing third-grade children learning single-digit arithmetic
target_learning_goals: automatized retrieval of single-digit arithmetic facts
examples: The study used multiplication verification items with table-related false solutions (e.g., 6 × 3 = 24) to probe competing associations

title: Because neural mechanisms underlying similar behavioral performance can differ by group, assessments should examine underlying processing mechanisms rather than relying on behavior alone
description: The article argues that examining the neural systems underlying a cognitive ability can reveal distinct mechanisms behind similar behavioral performance: "examining the neural systems underlying a particular cognitive ability can identify different mechanisms that give rise to similar impairments in behavioral performance." target_learning_goals: accurate identification of which attentional mechanism (signal enhancement vs. distractor suppression) underlies a learner's difficulty

title: Adaptive strategy choice model (ASCM) of simple-arithmetic strategy selection and efficiency
description: The adaptive strategy choice model (ASCM) of Siegler and Shipley (1995), as described in this article, holds that people have several strategies available and choose the fastest and most accurate one, governed by a confidence criterion determining how sure they must be to state a retrieved answer and a search length determining how many retrieval attempts are made before switching to a procedural strategy. title: Association-building explanations for why the testing effect decreases with material complexity
description: The review advances an explanatory account built on two existing explanations for low element interactivity materials: free recall improves retention through organization of information during recall, and paired-associate testing strengthens memory traces via mediators. Both hinge on "elaborative processes that establish relations between information elements", which are less necessary when such relations are inherent to complex material, and restudy may instead afford relational processing of elements while maintaining student motivation.
requirements: The account assumes testing benefits arise mainly from establishing associations between elements during retrieval
constraints: The review notes "very few studies have systematically evaluated theoretical explanations for the memorial benefits of testing"

title: ASReview open-source machine-learning abstract screening software
description: ASReview is an open-source machine-learning tool for abstract screening in systematic reviews, used in this study's retrospective simulation. The article states that "the ASReview software, an open-source platform, provides multiple learning algorithms for both feature extraction and classification." Researchers install it, load a study database (titles and abstracts), classify a small initial subset, then choose a feature extraction method, classifier, balancing strategy (default dynamic resampling), and query strategy (default certainty-based sampling). The algorithm iteratively suggests the study predicted most relevant for the reviewer's include/exclude decision.

citation: Sara Berti, Valentina Grazia, Luisa Molinari. (2023). Active Student Participation in Whole-School Interventions in Secondary School. A Systematic Literature Review. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-023-09773-x
title: Five-level scale of Active Student Participation (ASP) in whole-school intervention activities
description: The review proposes an organizing structure that grades program activities on a 5-point scale of active student participation, partly following the school participation scale of the HBSC questionnaire (De Róiste et al., 2012). As the review states, "It ranged from Very high levels of ASP, attributed to activities in which students were given a fully decision-making role, to Very low levels of ASP, given to activities in which students were just the recipients of activities delivered by adults." Very high ASP covers decision-making processes and school action teams with students; high ASP covers student artifacts, student-led activities for peers and for adults; moderate ASP covers platforms, interactive assemblies and data collection; low ASP covers trainings, group and individual activities within adult-designed formats. Levels are not mutually exclusive, and coding was based on the qualitative analysis of students' role, not the number of students involved.
requirements: Activities must be coded by qualitative analysis of the role attributed to students, not by the number of students involved
Levels are not mutually exclusive, so each program may include different levels of ASP
constraints: In the reviewed sample, no program involved students solely as passive recipients (Very low ASP), since such studies were excluded by the inclusion criteria

target_learning_goals: student participation in school activities and decision-making
improving the school learning environment
examples: The review coded all 13 programs on this scale (Table 5): e.g., SEHER included activities at every level from decision-making committees to teacher-led workshops, while STAC's activities were limited to peer-leader trainings

citation: Jessica Massonnié, Maryse Bianco, Laurent Lima, Pascal Bressoux. (2018). Longitudinal predictors of reading comprehension in French at first grade: Unpacking the oral comprehension component of the simple view. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.learninstruc.2018.01.005

description: The article recommends a fine-grained conceptualisation of oral comprehension in early reading instruction and assessment. citation: Autin, Frédérique; Batruch, Anatolia; Butera, Fabrizio. (2019). The function of selection of assessment leads evaluators to artificially create the social class achievement gap. Journal of Educational Psychology. https://doi.org/10.1037/edu0000307

examples: Participants graded a test attributed to a high- or low-SES student using normative grading or formative comments; the low-SES penalty appeared under normative grading and was reduced under formative comments.

title: Assess a learner's prior knowledge before teaching new content
description: Because prior knowledge steers learning in ways that depend on activation, relevance, and congruency, the article concludes that assessing what a learner already knows remains essential before instruction. title: Astus's knowledge-based system: a knowledge representation approach in which each type of knowledge unit has a clearly defined semantic on which the MTT's pedagogical module can rely
description: Astus is a model-tracing tutor (MTT) framework whose knowledge-based system models the task as the teacher's instructions rather than as the procedural knowledge of an ideal learner. target_learning_goals: multi-step problem-solving strategies
efficient proof construction
domain rule application
examples: In the Deep Thought tutor, students in the treatment condition received Assertions after about 40% of their steps, resulting in 3-4 hints per problem given the mean 9-step training solutions.

description: The review used ASReview (Active learning for Systematic Reviews), a machine-learning-based tool to conduct systematic reviews. target_learning_goals: understanding how study design choices affect the validity of impact estimates

title: The 'Asegúrate' program is structured around three main pillars: normative social behavior, self-regulation skills, and adolescent ideas/beliefs
description: The 'Asegúrate' program is a teacher-implemented intervention against cyberbullying and its associated risks. constraints: The program primarily works in virtual environments, though results demonstrate transfer of control to physical environments.

target_learning_goals: Reduce involvement in cyber-aggression, bullying aggression, sexting, and abusive use of the Internet and social networks
examples: The program's activity sequence identifies pre-existing ideas about virtual environments, analyzes behavior, reflects on reasons and consequences, and generalizes achievements to other relationship contexts.

title: Focus communication assessment on the patient's frame of reference rather than the physician's words
description: The MAAS 2.0 revision systematically shifts item wording toward the patient's perspective: summarizing should use "the patient's words" rather than the physician's own words, and information transfer should occur "within the patient's reference framework". requirements: Assessors must evaluate whether information transfer takes place within the patient's reference framework and whether summaries use the patient's words
constraints: Grounded in the context of GP consultations as described in this report; the authors note the formative implementation in postgraduate feedback remains to be examined

title: Assess POCUS trainees in the workplace on real patients in real time, because simulated assessments miss real clinical contexts
description: The article argues that OSCE-style assessments using simulated pathology videos or mannequins are limited compared with real cases, and that a year of real-practice assessments showed "the measurable benefits of a POCUS course being integrated into real clinical practice". examples: Researchers staff rated 3014 real-patient ultrasound clips and images recorded by residents during one year of on-shift clinical practice at Srinagarind Hospital

article_title: The role of virtual reality simulation in surgical training in the light of COVID-19 pandemic: Visual spatial ability as a predictor for improved surgical performance: a randomized trial.
citation: Sommer GM, Broschewitz J, Huppert S, Sommer CG, Jahn N, Jansen-Winkeln B, Gockel I, Hau HM. (2021). The role of virtual reality simulation in surgical training in the light of COVID-19 pandemic: Visual spatial ability as a predictor for improved surgical performance: a randomized trial. Medicine. https://doi.org/10.1097/MD.0000000000027844
title: Assess visual spatial ability with a simple test to identify training needs in surgical novices
description: The article concludes that VSA assessment is practical and informative for surgical education: "Assessing VSA with a simple test is feasible and high VSA scores indicate superior surgical spatial performance in VR simulator tasks." Because VSA correlates with performance mainly at the start of training, identifying VSA levels allows training needs analysis at the individual level, while low-VSA trainees can be expected to catch up with structured practice.
requirements: A validated VSA instrument such as the tube figure test, administered before curriculum training.
constraints: The article cautions that whether future residency performance can be predicted from VSA remains unclear, and that pre-existing advantages can be outweighed by training and experience.
target_learners: surgical novices
medical students entering surgical training
target_learning_goals: prediction of initial laparoscopic performance
individualized training needs analysis
examples: In the trial, all 60 participants passed the tube figure test on day 1 and again on day 9, and the training group was median-split into high- and low-VSA subgroups for learning-curve analysis.
